title: Spreadsheet and report automation agent
tagline: Turns a folder of messy Excel, CSV and Google Sheets exports into one clean monthly report with charts, a written summary and a full audit trail.
pitch: Every month somebody on your team opens five spreadsheets from five people, fixes the headers, the dates and the product codes by hand, pastes them together and writes the same report. I built an agent that does that work in about a second: you drop the files in a folder, and it gives back an Excel report with charts, a web page, a written summary, a list of every row it could not use and a log of every fix it made. The numbers are computed by code, never by the language model, so the same files always give the same report. On 100 test files spoiled at random it recovered every order line, where a standard script recovered none.
problem: Small and mid-sized companies run on spreadsheets that different people export in different shapes: title rows above the header, different column names, dates and prices typed in three formats, product codes with typos, totals rows and duplicates. Building the monthly report means hours of manual cleaning, and nobody can say afterwards which rows were changed or left out.
solution: A Python pipeline with a language model in two small, checked roles. Code finds the header row, maps each column to a standard field, parses dates, numbers and product codes, joins the sales files to the product list and the targets, sets aside the rows it cannot trust, computes the figures and builds an Excel report and a web report. The language model is asked only what a column means when the rules cannot tell, and its answer is used only if the values in the column fit. It can also write the summary paragraph, with every number checked against the computed figures, but the template writes it by default because the test showed a small model attaching correct numbers to wrong statements. The report works with no model at all.
features: Reads .xlsx workbooks (every visible sheet), .csv files with any common delimiter and encoding, and Google Sheets by link
Finds the real header row under title banners and leaves out totals rows, repeated headers, blank rows and note lines
Maps differently named columns to one standard schema with five methods: memory of earlier runs, name, arithmetic, value profile, and the language model for leftovers
Tells a unit price from a line total by how the values behave per product, even when the header is misleading
Parses dates, prices and quantities written in several national formats and decides day-first or month-first per column
Repairs product codes against the product list (case, spaces, separators, O typed for 0) and reports the ones it cannot match
Sets aside unusable rows with the file, the row number, the reason and the original content instead of dropping them silently
Removes lines exported twice, and warns when a file has no order numbers to detect them
Compares the month with the previous month and with the targets per region
Produces an Excel workbook with nine sheets and three native charts, a self-contained web report with interactive charts, and a summary ready for email
Checks every number in a model-written summary against the computed figures and falls back to the template
Remembers what the model decided about a column name, so it is asked once and a person can correct it
Runs from one command, from cron, or from a small upload page

stack.name: pandas
stack.role: Holds the tables, joins them and computes every figure in the report.
stack.why: It is the standard tool for tabular data in Python, so any data engineer can maintain the project. A database was not needed for files of this size.

stack.name: openpyxl
stack.role: Reads Excel workbooks cell by cell and writes the Excel report with native charts.
stack.why: Reading cell by cell lets the agent see title rows and totals rows that pandas.read_excel would mix into the data. Native charts stay editable in Excel, unlike pasted images.

stack.name: Plotly
stack.role: Draws the three interactive charts of the web report, in a light and a dark version.
stack.why: The charts work in any browser from a single file with no server, and the reader can hover to see exact values. Matplotlib would give static images only.

stack.name: Jinja2
stack.role: Fills the web report template and escapes any text that comes from the files.
stack.why: Automatic escaping prevents a cell containing HTML from breaking or hijacking the report page.

stack.name: OpenAI API client (optional)
stack.role: Asks a language model what a leftover column means, and optionally to write the summary.
stack.why: The client is OpenAI-compatible, so the same code runs on OpenAI, Azure OpenAI or a local model through Ollama. The default provider is a mock that needs no key.

stack.name: FastAPI + Uvicorn
stack.role: Serve the upload page and the run endpoint.
stack.why: Small, typed, and it validates uploads and documents its own API. Flask would need more code for the same checks.

stack.name: pytest
stack.role: 118 offline tests for every parser, every mapping method, the guardrails and the whole pipeline.
stack.why: The tests run with no key and no network, so a client or reviewer can check the project in half a minute.

workflow.detail: The agent lists the spreadsheet files in the given folders and downloads any Google Sheets link as CSV. A file that cannot be opened is reported and the run continues with the others.

Each sheet is read as raw cells. The header is the first wide row made only of labels with data under it. Banners above it, blank rows, repeated headers, totals rows and note lines are left out, and their row numbers are logged.

The product list and the targets are recognised first, because their codes and region names help to read the sales files. Each sales column is then matched to a standard field by memory, by name, by arithmetic (amount = quantity x price), by what its values look like, and last by the language model. Whatever the method, the values must fit the field.

The date order and the decimal mark are decided once per column from all its values. Dates, numbers and product codes are converted; a missing total, price or quantity is computed from the other two. Rows without a code, a readable date or a usable amount are set aside with the reason.
Sales lines from all files are stacked, lines exported twice are removed, lines outside the report month are set aside, and each line gets its product name, category and cost from the product list.

pandas computes revenue, units, orders, average order, margin and returns, the split by region and by category, the top products, the daily trend, the share of each target reached and the change on the previous month taken from the history file.

The figures are turned into a fact sheet. The template writes the summary from it. If the model is asked to write it, code checks every number in its text against the fact sheet, gives it one retry, and otherwise uses the template.
The agent writes the Excel workbook, the web page, the summary text and the run log into a folder for the month, and saves the month's headline figures for next month's comparison.

phases.name: Foundation
phases.goal: A repository that runs, realistic messy demo files with a known correct answer, and a naive baseline to beat.

steps.text: Create the repository skeleton, the virtual environment and pinned requirements
Write the data generator: a garden-supplies wholesaler with three regions, a product list and targets, plus the clean truth
Write the mess generator: banners, renamed columns, mixed date and number formats, typos, totals rows, duplicates, bad rows
Write the file readers for xlsx, csv and Google Sheets links
Write the naive baseline (default pandas readers and exact column names) and measure it against the truth

phases.outcome: A git repository with pinned dependencies; a generator that writes two months of fictional sales for a garden-supplies wholesaler (three branches, 48 products, targets) together with the clean truth; a mess generator with 17 kinds of defect; readers for xlsx, csv and Google Sheets links that return the raw grid of cells; and a naive baseline (default pandas readers) that recovers 0% of the demo rows, because every demo file has a banner, text-formatted numbers or unknown headers.

phases.name: Core
phases.goal: The cleaning pipeline works end to end on the mock provider.

steps.text: Header row detection and removal of banners, totals, repeated headers and blank rows
Column mapping by alias, similar spelling and value profile, with the language-model step for leftovers
Value parsers for dates, numbers and product codes with per-column format inference
Stacking, duplicate removal, joins to products and targets, and the rejected-rows list
The orchestrator that runs the steps in order and records every decision

phases.outcome: The pipeline runs end to end with no model: it finds the header row, maps the columns (by name, by arithmetic, by value profile, and by the language model for leftovers), parses dates, numbers and product codes with the format decided per column, removes duplicates, joins the product list and targets, and lists every rejected row with its reason. On both demo months it recovers 100% of the true order lines with every value exact.

phases.name: Report
phases.goal: The cleaned data becomes a report a manager can read.

steps.text: Figures: totals, splits by region and category, top products, daily trend, comparison with last month and with targets
Written summary: template version, language-model version and the number check
Excel workbook with native charts, clean data, rejected rows, column mapping and audit log
Web report with interactive charts
History file so that next month's run can compare with this one

phases.outcome: One command builds the report for a month: an Excel workbook with nine sheets and three native charts (summary, regions, categories, top products, daily figures, clean data, rejected rows, column mapping, audit log), a self-contained web page with three interactive charts that follows the reader's light or dark theme, a summary text file and a run log. The summary is written from a fact sheet and every number in it is checked by code. Each run saves the month's figures, so the September report shows +6.2% against August.

phases.name: Quality
phases.goal: Measured accuracy on files the pipeline has not seen, and guardrails for the model.

steps.text: Benchmark of randomly generated messy files with known truth
Metrics: header detection, column mapping (seen and unseen names), row recovery, revenue error, rejected-row precision and recall
Compare with the naive baseline on the same files
Fix the defects the benchmark finds and re-run
Error handling: unreadable files, sheets with no table, missing product list, model failures

phases.outcome: A benchmark that spoils sales files at random and scores the cleaning against the known truth, next to a naive pandas baseline. It found four real defects, all fixed: a crash on files with no quantity column, files skipped when only two of quantity, price and total were present under unfamiliar names, a price-like header that was really a line total, and sheets of one workbook being read separately. 107 offline tests cover every parser, every mapping method, the model guardrails and the failure cases (broken file, unknown table, missing product list, model outage).

phases.name: Interface
phases.goal: One command for the demo, a schedulable command for real use, and an upload page.

steps.text: Command line: demo, run, and make-data commands with a readable step-by-step log
FastAPI upload page: drop files, run, view and download the report
Google Sheets link test against a local web server
Schedule example (cron) for the recurring run

phases.outcome: Three ways to run it: 'python -m sheetagent demo' builds two months of reports from generated files in about three seconds; 'python -m sheetagent run <files, folders or Google Sheets links>' is the command a scheduler calls, with a cron script that builds last month's report; and 'python -m sheetagent serve' opens an upload page where a non-technical person drops the files and gets the web report and the Excel file back. Reading a table from a link is tested against a local web server, and the upload page was run in a real browser.

phases.name: Verification and docs
phases.goal: Everything is tested, measured, and explained.

steps.text: Full pytest run, offline
Fresh-clone run of the quick start
Real-model check (OpenAI if a key is present, otherwise a local model through the same client)
README with diagram, real output, screenshot and results table
Complete the dashboard entry: decisions, client questions, concepts, limits
Secret scan and final commit

phases.outcome: 118 tests pass offline. A fresh clone installed from requirements.txt runs the demo and the tests. The final benchmark on an unseen seed recovers 100% of order lines on 100 files. The OpenAI check is pending because the key was empty; the same client code was run on a local model instead, which showed that the model is useful for naming columns (19 to 30 perfect files out of 30) and unreliable for writing the summary (4 of 6 wrong in wording), so the template became the default writer. README, license and this dashboard entry are complete.

decisions.title: A fixed plan of steps, not a free tool-calling agent
decisions.chosen: The agent always runs the same eight steps in the same order. The judgement calls happen inside the steps and are written to a trace.
decisions.why: A monthly report must be reproducible: the same files must give the same numbers, and a manager must be able to see why a row was left out. A fixed plan gives that, and it is testable step by step.

alternatives.option: Let a language model decide which tool to call next (ReAct-style agent)
alternatives.why_not: The result can change between runs, each run costs many model calls, and an earlier build showed the small local model calling tools on every request. For a recurring report that is risk with no benefit.

alternatives.option: Ask the model to write pandas code for each file
alternatives.why_not: Running generated code on business files needs a sandbox, and a wrong line of code produces wrong totals that look right.

decisions.at_scale: With dozens of report types I would keep the fixed steps and move the per-client knowledge (schemas, aliases, checks) into configuration, and add a review queue for the decisions the agent is unsure about.

decisions.title: Rules first, the model only for leftover columns
decisions.chosen: Columns are mapped by memory, name, arithmetic and value profile. The model is asked only about columns that none of these can place, with the header and five sample values.
decisions.why: On 100 benchmark files the rules alone placed every column they attempted correctly and cost nothing. The model then lifted never-seen column names from 68.4% to 93.9% on a 30-file sample, at 47 short calls.

alternatives.option: Send every header to the model
alternatives.why_not: It is slower (about 12 seconds per file on the local model instead of 0.2), costs money on every run, and the model was wrong on about one column in ten, which the rules never were.
A quarter of never-seen column names stay unread, mostly the order number, and then duplicate lines cannot be detected.

decisions.at_scale: I would log every model decision for a person to confirm once, and promote confirmed names into the alias list so the model is needed less each month.

decisions.title: Every model answer about a column is checked against the values
decisions.chosen: A column is accepted for a field only if its values fit: dates must parse as dates, a quantity proposed by anything weaker than an exact header must be whole numbers, a region proposed by the model must contain known regions.
decisions.why: The live check caught the model labelling a warehouse column (W1, W2) as the region in 3 of 30 files, which moved sales to a region that does not exist. With the value check that answer is refused.

alternatives.why_not: One wrong label silently changes a regional total.

alternatives.option: Ask the model for a confidence score and use a threshold
alternatives.why_not: Small models report high confidence on wrong answers; a check on the data is evidence, a self-reported score is not.

decisions.at_scale: More fields would get their own value checks (customer names against the CRM, order numbers against the ERP).

decisions.title: Tell a price from a total by behaviour, not by the header
decisions.chosen: When quantity, price and total are all present, the relation amount = quantity x price decides which column is which. When only one money column is present, the agent checks whether its values stay stable per product (a unit price) or scale with the quantity (a line total).
decisions.why: Headers lie: 'Ext. Price' looks like a price and is a line total. The benchmark found this defect, and the behaviour test fixed it without adding the name to a list.

alternatives.option: Keep extending the list of known header names
alternatives.why_not: It never ends, and it cannot be measured honestly, because the test names would be the ones in the list.
The data already contains the answer, for free and with certainty.

decisions.at_scale: The same idea extends to tax, discount and freight columns, each with its own arithmetic relation.

decisions.title: The template writes the summary by default, the model only on request
decisions.chosen: The summary paragraph comes from a template filled with computed figures. '--summary model' lets the model write it; code then checks every number against the fact sheet, allows one retry, and falls back to the template.
decisions.why: All 6 summaries written by the local model passed the number check, yet 4 of the 6 said something false when I read them, such as calling growth on last month a margin over target. A number check cannot see that, so the safe default is the template.

alternatives.option: Model-written summary by default, guarded by the number check
alternatives.why_not: Measured in this build: the guard passes text that is wrong in meaning.
A stronger model may write well, and some clients want a more natural text. Keeping it as a labelled option lets them try it knowingly.

decisions.at_scale: I would test a stronger model on the same six cases, and add a second check that ties each number to the kind of fact it came from before making it the default.

decisions.title: Set rows aside with a reason instead of guessing or dropping
decisions.chosen: A row with no product code, an unreadable date or no usable amount goes to a 'Rejected rows' sheet with its file, row number, reason and original content. Sales of a product missing from the product list are kept in the totals under their own label.
decisions.why: A report that silently drops rows cannot be trusted, and one that guesses values is worse. The person who owns the source file can fix the 16 listed rows in a minute.

alternatives.option: Drop bad rows silently, as pandas does with errors='coerce'
alternatives.why_not: Revenue disappears and nobody knows why the total differs from the ERP.

alternatives.option: Fill missing values with a guess (last date seen, average price)

decisions.at_scale: The rejected rows would go back to each branch automatically as a short correction list.

decisions.title: Decide date order and decimal mark per column
decisions.chosen: The agent looks at all values of a column: a day above 12 settles day-first or month-first; if no value settles it, the reading that puts the dates inside the report month wins. Decimal comma or point is decided by majority.
decisions.why: '03/04/2026' and '1.234' cannot be read alone. Reading each cell separately, as pandas does by default, mixes two interpretations in one column.

alternatives.why_not: This is the naive baseline, which recovered 0% of the benchmark rows.

alternatives.option: Ask the user for the format of each file
alternatives.why_not: That is the manual work the tool is meant to remove; the choice is logged instead, so it can be reviewed.

decisions.at_scale: The format decided for a source would be stored and reused, with an alert when a source suddenly changes format.

decisions.title: Native Excel charts and a single-file web page
decisions.chosen: The workbook contains real Excel charts linked to its data sheets; the web report is one HTML file with the chart library inside.
decisions.why: Managers forward reports by email and edit them in Excel. Native charts stay editable, and a single file opens anywhere, offline.

alternatives.option: A hosted dashboard (Power BI, Looker, Streamlit)
alternatives.why_not: It needs licences, hosting and logins. It is the right next step for some clients, and the clean data sheet is ready to feed it.
They cannot be edited and do not follow the data if a figure is corrected.

decisions.at_scale: The clean rows would also be loaded into a warehouse table, so a BI tool can sit on top while the emailed report stays.

decisions.title: Tune on some seeds, report on one never seen
decisions.chosen: The rules were fixed using benchmark seeds 11 and 2026. The published result uses seed 4242, and the model comparison uses seed 5151, neither of which was looked at before.
decisions.why: Fixing a rule and then reporting on the same files measures memory, not ability. The first seeds exposed four defects; the unseen seed showed whether the fixes generalise.

alternatives.option: Report the score on the files used for tuning
alternatives.why_not: It would be an inflated number.

alternatives.option: Use real company spreadsheets as the test
alternatives.why_not: Client data must not be used, and real files have no known correct answer to score against.

decisions.at_scale: Each client project would start by collecting a few months of their real files, hand-checking the totals once, and keeping them as a regression set.

client_qa.q: How much time does this save us?
client_qa.a: The cleaning and assembling that takes a person several hours each month runs in about a second per month of files. What remains for a person is reading the short list of rows the agent set aside, 16 out of 878 in the demo, and fixing them at the source if they matter.

Yes, for three reasons. The numbers are computed by ordinary code from the cleaned rows, never by the AI. Nothing is dropped silently: every row left out is listed with its file, row number and reason, and every repair is counted in an audit sheet. And on 100 test files with known correct answers, the tool recovered every order line exactly.

client_qa.q: Our files change all the time: new columns, renamed headers, a different export. Will it break?
client_qa.a: It is built for that. It does not rely on a column being in a given place or having an exact name. It recognises columns by name, by close spelling, by arithmetic and by what the values look like, and can ask a language model for the rest. In the test, three quarters of column names it had never been told about were read correctly with no AI, and 94% with a small AI model. If it cannot identify what it needs, it says so and skips that table rather than guessing.

client_qa.q: Do our data leave the company?
client_qa.a: By default nothing leaves: the tool runs with no AI model and no internet connection. If you switch the model on, it is sent only a column header with five sample values, and the computed totals for the summary, never the rows. It can also use a model running on your own server, which is how I tested it.

client_qa.q: What does it cost to run?
client_qa.a: Without the model, nothing beyond the machine it runs on. With a hosted model the usage is tiny: the test used about 7,000 input tokens for 30 files, which is a fraction of a cent on a small OpenAI model. I have not run it on OpenAI yet, so that figure is an estimate from the token count, not a measured bill.

client_qa.q: Is this really AI, or just a script? Why not let ChatGPT read the files?
client_qa.a: It is mostly careful code, on purpose. A language model reading 900 rows will sometimes change a number, cannot explain which row it dropped, and gives a slightly different answer each time. So the AI is used where it is strong, understanding what an oddly named column means, and its answer is checked against the data. I also tested letting it write the summary: the text read well, but four out of six contained a false statement. That is why the default summary comes from a template.

client_qa.q: Can it work with our real report instead of sales by region?
client_qa.a: Yes. The reading, cleaning and auditing parts are general. What is specific is the list of fields (a small file) and the figures of the report. Adapting it to purchases, inventory, timesheets or marketing spend means describing the fields and writing the calculations, typically a few days of work with your real files.

client_qa.q: Does it work with Google Sheets, and with Power BI or Looker?
client_qa.a: It reads a Google Sheet from its link when the sheet is shared by link; private sheets need a service account, which I would add for a real project. For Power BI, Tableau or Looker, the 'Clean data' sheet is exactly the tidy table those tools need, so the agent can feed them instead of replacing them.

client_qa.q: How does it know whether 03/04/2026 is the third of April or the fourth of March?
client_qa.a: It looks at the whole column. If any date has a day above 12, the order is settled for the column. If none does, it picks the reading that puts the dates in the month being reported. The choice and its reason are written in the audit log.

client_qa.q: What happens when a product code is mistyped?
client_qa.a: Codes are compared with the product list after removing differences of case, spaces, separators and leading zeros. A letter O typed for a zero is repaired only if exactly one product matches. A code that still matches nothing is kept in the totals under 'Not in product list' and flagged, because the sale is real even if the product list is behind.

client_qa.q: How do we run it every month without thinking about it?
client_qa.a: It is one command, so any scheduler can call it. A cron script is included that builds last month's report from a folder named after the month. It keeps each month's headline figures, so the next report shows the change automatically.

It expects a header row and one table per sheet, a calendar month as the period, and one currency. It does not read old .xls files or protected workbooks. And the test files, although spoiled in seventeen ways, were generated by me: the first step with a client is to run it on a few months of their real files and check the totals against a report they trust.

Three ways. There are 118 automated tests, including what happens when a file is broken or the AI is unavailable. A benchmark spoils files at random and compares the result with the known truth, next to a standard script as a baseline; I tuned on some random draws and reported on one I had not seen. And I ran the AI path on a real model and read its output by hand, which is how I found that its summaries could not be trusted.

concepts.plain: Finding which row of a sheet holds the column titles. Real exports put a title, a date or a company name above it, so the first row cannot be assumed.

The fixed list of things the report needs from every file: order number, date, product code, quantity, unit price, amount, customer, region. Every file is translated to this list, whatever its own column names are.
Deciding which column of a file corresponds to which standard field. 'Qty', 'Pieces' and 'Quantité' all map to quantity.
A known spelling of a field name, such as 'Invoice #' for the order number. The rules recognise aliases immediately; other names need the smarter methods.
Comparing two texts by how similar they are instead of requiring them to be identical. It lets 'Ammount' be recognised as 'Amount'.
A description of what a column contains: what share of its cells are dates, numbers, whole numbers, product codes. A column that is 97% dates is a date column whatever its title says.
Using the relation amount = quantity x unit price to identify columns. If one number column equals the product of two others on nearly every row, the roles of the three are known with certainty.
Turning inconsistent raw data into one consistent format: the same date format, real numbers instead of text like '$1,234.50', the same spelling for each product code.
In much of Europe 1.234,50 means one thousand two hundred thirty-four and a half; in the US the same number is written 1,234.50. The tool decides which convention a column uses from all its values.
The short code that identifies a product, such as HT-0101. Matching codes across files is how sales lines get their product name, category and cost.
Combining two tables through a shared key. Here each sales line is joined to the product list through the product code, like a VLOOKUP done for every row at once.
Removing a line that appears twice because a file was exported or pasted twice. It is done only when an order number proves the two lines are the same sale.
Rows that cannot be used safely are set aside in their own sheet with the reason, instead of being deleted or guessed. The owner of the source file can then fix them.
A record of every change the tool made and every decision it took: which row was the header, how each column was read, how many codes were repaired. It lets anyone verify the report afterwards.
Key performance indicator: a headline number a manager follows, such as revenue, number of orders or margin.
Revenue minus what the goods cost to buy. The tool computes it from the unit cost in the product list.
Actual revenue divided by the target for the same region and month. 93.8% means the region ended 6.2% short of its goal.
The change of a figure compared with the previous month, in percent.
The kind of AI behind ChatGPT: it reads and writes text. Here it is used to understand what an unusually named column means.
A program that carries a task through several steps and makes decisions along the way. This one follows a fixed plan and records each decision, which makes its results repeatable.
A check that code applies to an AI answer before using it. Here: a column label is accepted only if the column's values fit, and a number in the summary only if it exists in the computed figures.
When a language model states something that is not in the data it was given. The summary test showed a subtle form: real numbers attached to the wrong statement.
Reading the model's text back and verifying that each number appears in the facts it was given. It catches invented and rounded figures, but not a correct figure used in a wrong sentence.
A stand-in for the AI model that needs no key and no internet. It lets anyone run and test the project for free, and shows what the tool does with no AI at all.
A common way of talking to language models that many providers and local tools support. Because the tool uses it, switching from OpenAI to a model on your own server is a setting, not a rewrite.
Software that runs a language model on your own machine, so no data leaves it. It was used here to test the AI path at no cost.
The simple approach a result is compared with, here a standard pandas script. Without a baseline, a score has no meaning.
Test cases that were not looked at while building. Reporting on them shows whether the tool handles new files, not only the ones it was tuned on.
Data generated by a script instead of taken from a company. It contains no real information, and because the correct answer is known, the cleaning can be scored exactly.
Extract, transform, load: reading data from sources, cleaning and reshaping it, and delivering it somewhere useful. This project is a small ETL pipeline whose output is a report.
The scheduler built into Linux servers. One line tells it to run the report command on the second day of every month.

limits: The schema covers sales lines, a product list and monthly targets. Another kind of report needs its own fields and its own calculations.

The benchmark files and the cleaning rules were written by the same author. The results show the rules handle the defects the generator knows; real company files will contain others, and that has not been measured.
No real company spreadsheets were used (client data is not allowed in this portfolio), so the first step of a real project is a check against a report the client already trusts.
A sheet must have a header row. Tables without headers, two tables side by side on one sheet, and pivot layouts with months as columns are not handled.
Old .xls files and password-protected workbooks are not read. Formula cells are read as the last value Excel calculated.

Google Sheets are read through the CSV export link, so the sheet must be shared as 'anyone with the link'. Private sheets need a service account, which is not included. The link reader was tested against a local web server, not against Google.
No currency conversion: if files carry different currency marks the report warns and adds the amounts as written.

Duplicate lines are removed only in files with an order-number column. Without the model, a quarter of unfamiliar column names (mostly order numbers) stay unread, which left duplicates in 19 of 100 benchmark files.
A model-written summary can pass the number check and still be wrong in meaning (4 of 6 on the local model). The template is the default writer for that reason.
The real-model results come from a small local model (llama3.2, 3B). OpenAI models were not run because the key was empty, so their accuracy and cost here are unknown.
The model comparison uses 30 files and the summary review 6 cases: enough to see the direction, too few for precise percentages.
The report period is a calendar month and the comparison is with the previous month only (no year-over-year, no weekly report).
The upload page has no login and keeps each run separately, so it shows no month-over-month comparison except in the demo. It is meant for use on localhost or behind the client's own access control.
Quantities under a column whose name is only similar to a known one must be whole numbers; goods sold by weight need an exact header such as 'Quantity' or 'Qty'.
run: python -m sheetagent run <files, folders or Google Sheets links> --period 2026-09 --out reports
python -m sheetagent serve   (upload page on http://127.0.0.1:8124)

verification.notes: The OpenAI live check is pending: OPENAI_API_KEY in /var/www/AB/github-projects/.env was empty during the build, so no request was sent and nothing was spent. The real-model path (the same OpenAI-compatible client) was run at no cost on local llama3.2 (3B) through Ollama. Column naming: on 30 files of an unseen seed, never-seen column names read correctly rose from 68.4% to 93.9%, and files with no error from 19 to 30 of 30, in 47 calls (7,048 input and 112 output tokens). A first run on another seed found a real defect: the model labelled a warehouse column as the region in 3 of 30 files; a value check now refuses that, and a test covers it. Summary writing: 6 of 6 model summaries passed the automatic number check, but read by hand only 2 of 6 were correct; the template was therefore made the default writer and the model summary an option that is labelled for review. End to end through the command line on the local model: 3 calls, 53 seconds, report produced. Also verified: the benchmark found four defects in the rules, all fixed, and the final numbers come from a seed not used for tuning; a fresh clone installed from requirements.txt ran the demo and passed the tests; the upload page was run in a real browser (headless Chrome) and returned the demo report; the Excel workbook was opened with LibreOffice and its charts rendered; the cron script built a report. Not verified: reading a live Google Sheet (the link reader was tested against a local web server). To finish the pending check: put a key in .env and run `LLM_PROVIDER=openai python -m evals.run --files 30 --seed 5151 --provider openai` and `python -m evals.summary_check --provider openai --months 6` (estimated at under one cent on gpt-4o-mini from the token counts above).
